rv.q: A disjointed evening begins to generate an authentic sense of the tragic.
For good and for ill, though, it’s as painless a Lear as you’ll see.
This is a bare-bones Lear – stripped of much of its weird cosmic poetry and shorn too of much of its complexity.
His take on “the actor’s Everest” lacks both grandeur and pathos until its final third.
As a production it is packed with action and deft in its fight scenes, but remains rather flat, and perhaps unwilling to plumb this play’s tragic depths.
But despite its strengths, this is a staging that crucially misses the pathos and scope of this harrowing, humane play.

This unwise tactic has been playing to diminishing returns for years now and fatally undermines his take on one of the most iconic roles in Shakespeare, a role Branagh fans have been longing to see him assume.
On the evidence here, Branagh also needs a good director.
Not only confusing, by trying to fast-track the play's epic emotional journey, the spectacle becomes ever more bizarre and uncomfortable to watch.
This is less King Lear and more King Ken.
Instead, this production mostly feels meaningless and mechanical, with even the notorious, horrific eye-gouging scene stubbornly unmoving.
Branagh as Lear is a performance that deserves the West End hype, and maybe even (whisper it) the ticket prices.
Though it doesn’t explore its meaning (or find much of the humour that is also there), its brevity and its clear storyline could be a good introduction to the play.
But his King Lear, much-awaited, is a misfire.
Ultimately, it feels like a trial run and that Branagh’s Lear is still to come.
The main failing of Branagh’s performance is his bubbling, effervescent energy.
Gripping at the level of narrative but loose in its grasp of the play’s poetic depth, this is an attractively, if unevenly, packaged version King Lear.
More a brief sojourn into mid-life crisis eccentricity than tragic mental disintegration.
A fantastic take on a new facet of a timeless classic.

cn.t: Branagh's self-directed Lear divides critics, with most finding the brisk two-hour production lacks emotional depth and grandeur. His performance earns praise for clarity and energy, but the stripped-down staging feels rushed and hollow.
